- Peak concurrent inference workers: ~2,000 (90th percentile peak windows)

2) What guardrails do you recommend for shoulder buffering vs ephemeral burst pools?
3) How is billing handled for transient burst use vs reserved capacity?

I've attached a short SLO spreadsheet and our traffic sample. Procurement will need these details for the SOW. Can you share an ops-friendly runbook (eviction, preemption, fallback) and a line-item that we can include in the contract?

Thanks Simon — copied our Capacity & Ops leads so we can be concrete. Quick answers up front, then an ask for one traffic sample we couldn't parse.

High level proposal (ballpark):
- Initial reserved slab: 16 A100-ish eq GPUs (reserved) — supports baseline ~20 QPS with room for model variants and caching.
- Shoulder buffer: an additional 30% headroom (configurable) as reserved warm capacity to absorb short surges — equivalent to ~5 GPUs kept warm but not billed as committed compute when idle (operational headroom).
- Ephemeral burst pool: separate opportunistic pool of 24 GPUs that can be allocated on demand across the region for up to 12 minutes per allocation before preemption; fallback routing to lower-latency hosted variants on sustained usage.

Rationale:
- Your peak 65 QPS with long contexts maps to spikes that are short-lived (minutes). We recommend a smaller reserved slab + shoulder buffer + larger ephemeral pool to minimize committed dollars while meeting 99.5% latency.

Billing model (proposal):
- Reserved slab: monthly committed charge (standard Dedicated fee line).
- Shoulder buffer: small retention fee (reserve-warm) to keep warm instances available (monthly, discounted) — only invoked when scaling out.
- Ephemeral burst: on-demand per-minute billing at a higher unit rate; disputed minutes above the monthly cap can be credited if we fail to provide capacity per SLA.

Action items:
- Ben: run a quick capacity-sensitivity calc using Vertex sample + model tokenization.
- Marcus: draft the ops runbook and eviction/preemption policy we can attach to the SOW.

I couldn't open the traffic sample ZIP — can you re-send the CSV of request timestamps and token counts?

Best,
Irene

I ran a quick back-of-envelope using the sample SLO sheet Simon sent. Notes:
- Assumptions: 450 tokens avg response, 350 tokens avg request = 800 tokens total per call. Using our A100 eq throughput median of ~1500 tokens/s (conservative for long-context, includes KV cache miss).
- Single GPU throughput: ~1.8 req/s (800 tokens * 1.8 req/s ≈ 1440 tokens/s) under mixed batch.

Sizing:
- Baseline 20 QPS -> ~12 GPUs to handle sustained baseline with 20% buffer for background tasks.
- Peak 65 QPS -> ~36 GPUs total if all peak sustained (unlikely).
- Practical plan: reserve 12 GPUs (baseline), configure shoulder buffer to keep 4 warm (instant scale), and allow ephemeral pool up to +28 GPUs for bursts. That gets us to 44 GPUs available during severe surges.

Notes on policies:
- Warm shoulder should have pre-warm KV caches for the most common prefixes (we can pre-warm based on recent traffic).
- Ephemeral allocations should have a short TTL (10-15 min) and be billed per-minute. If Vertex requires longer sustained access, we recommend temporarily promoting ephemeral to reserved (with a notice window).

I'll drop the calculation CSV: msr_capacity_calc_20281005.csv

Ben

Simon — answering operational questions inline:
1) TTL/Preemption: Ephemeral pools are best-effort but deterministic in behavior. We enforce a soft TTL (configurable) and a hard reclaim window. Soft TTL (10–15 min) will attempt graceful drain (stop accepting new requests, wait for in-flight to finish up to a 90s drain window). After soft TTL + drain we initiate hard preemption which will terminate instances. We guarantee the hard reclaim will occur within 2 minutes after the drain window. We'll document the exact sequence in the runbook.

2) Billing: Ephemeral billing will be a per-minute meterable charge on your monthly invoice with a separate line. We can structure a monthly burst credit (pool of minutes) at a discounted rate converted into an annual commitment — e.g., purchase a 10k-minute burst credit at 60% of on-demand per-minute. Any usage beyond the purchased credit is billed at the on-demand rate.

3) Shoulder buffer retention fee: yes, there is a small monthly retention fee to keep the shoulder buffer warm. If unused, the retention fee still applies because it reserves capacity within the region and keeps caches warm (we discount this fee relative to reserved slab).

Ops guarantees & credits: If Redwood fails to provide ephemeral capacity (e.g., pool fully saturated) and your traffic is routed to a lower-performing fallback beyond agreed SLOs, we can credit minutes of failed burst allocation at the on-demand rate (subject to a monthly cap and incident verification). We'll add an incident verification clause to the SOW — require Vertex to raise within 5 business days with traces.

I'll attach a draft short runbook and the eviction timeline into the SOW appendix tonight.

-Marcus
